opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest thing is that today's agent frameworks are still largely built *around* the model rather than *with* it. A lot of the scaffolding we see, the elaborate prompt chains, hand-written workflows, fixed tool-calling loops, exists because models weren't capable or reliable enough to manage long tasks themselves. So engineers wrapped them in a lot of external structure. That made sense as a transitional stage, but I don't think it's where things end up.

As models get stronger at reasoning, planning, and recovering from their own mistakes, a lot of that rigid orchestration should dissolve. The framework should become thinner and more about providing a good *environment* than prescribing the steps. What does the agent need? Reliable tools, a clean way to observe the results of its actions, memory that persists across sessions, and the ability to verify its own work. If you give a capable model those things, it can often figure out the workflow better than a human designer can hard-code it.

The second piece is that frameworks and training need to be connected much more tightly. Right now many agent frameworks are designed by people who aren't training the model, and models are trained without much knowledge of the frameworks they'll run in. That mismatch creates a lot of brittleness. Ideally, the environment an agent operates in during deployment should look very much like the environment it was trained in with reinforcement learning. Then the framework isn't just a runtime; it's also where the data and feedback signals come from, which closes the loop.

Third, I think we need to take long-horizon tasks seriously. Most current agents do fine on tasks that take minutes. But the really valuable work, like research, large software projects, or complex analysis, takes hours or days. That requires better context management, better ways for the agent to summarize and retrieve what it's done, and better checkpointing so it can recover from failures instead of starting over. Those are partly model problems and partly infrastructure problems.

And finally, evaluation. It's still very hard to tell whether an agent is genuinely good or just good on a benchmark. Frameworks should make it natural to measure real outcomes: did the code actually work, did the task actually get done, rather than just whether the trajectory looked reasonable.

So my short answer is that frameworks should become less about control and more about environment, feedback, and memory, and they should be co-designed with the models rather than bolted on afterward.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. That's a question I think about almost every day, so let me try to answer it honestly rather than neatly.

The first thing I'd say is that most of today's agent frameworks are still, at their core, orchestration layers. They decide which tool to call, in what order, how to pass context around, how to retry when something fails. That was necessary when models were weaker, because the model couldn't be trusted to hold a long plan in its head or recover from its own mistakes. So we built scaffolding around it. But a lot of that scaffolding is really a workaround for model limitations, and as the models get better, the scaffolding starts to get in the way. I've watched a lot of teams spend enormous effort tuning a framework, and then a new model release makes half of that effort unnecessary or even harmful, because the framework is constraining the model to a decomposition that no longer makes sense.

So the first evolution I expect is that frameworks will stop trying to be the brain and go back to being the body. Tool access, memory, sandboxing, permissions, observability, cost control. The things a model genuinely cannot do for itself. The planning and decomposition should move inside the model, and the framework should get out of the way.

The second thing is that model and agent can't really be designed separately anymore. In the early days you took a general chat model and bolted an agent loop on top. That's backwards. If you want an agent that works for an hour or a day on a task, the model has to be trained for that: for long-horizon credit assignment, for knowing when to stop and verify, for recognizing that it's stuck instead of looping. That's a training problem, not a prompting problem. So I think the frameworks that survive will be the ones built alongside the model, where the data generated by the agent running in the real environment flows back into training. Framework and model become one system that learns together.

Third, and this is where I think we're most behind: evaluation and trust. Right now we mostly evaluate agents on whether they completed a task. But if you're going to hand an agent real authority, access to your codebase, your accounts, your infrastructure, completion rate isn't enough. You need to know how it fails. Does it fail loudly or quietly? Does it ask before doing something irreversible? Can you audit what it did afterward? Frameworks need to make those properties first-class, not an afterthought. I'd rather have an agent that's a bit slower and tells me when it's uncertain than one that's fast and confidently wrong.

And the last point is about memory and continuity. Almost every agent today starts from zero each session. Humans don't work that way. A good colleague remembers what you cared about last week, remembers the mistake they made and the correction you gave. Getting that right is harder than it sounds, because you don't want the agent to accumulate junk or carry forward something that was true once and isn't anymore. But I think persistent, well-curated memory is going to be the difference between a tool you use and a collaborator you actually rely on.

So if I had to compress it: frameworks should become thinner and more trustworthy, models should absorb the planning, the two should be trained together, and the whole thing needs a real notion of memory and accountability. We're partway there on each of those, but not very far on any of them.

astra-6.text:
I think agent frameworks need to evolve together with models. Right now, a framework often compensates for what a model cannot reliably do: it breaks down tasks, manages context, calls tools, and checks results. As models improve, we should keep asking which of those structures are still useful and which have become constraints.

For me, the important direction is a tighter feedback loop between the model and the environment. An agent needs to understand whether an action actually worked, recognize when it has made a mistake, and adjust its approach. Producing a plausible sequence of steps is only part of that.

That also changes how we evaluate the system. Can it finish a long task? Can it recover from a failed tool call? Does it know when it needs clarification? I would like frameworks to make those behaviors easier to train and measure, while giving models room to develop better strategies.

sol-6.1.text:
I think agent frameworks need to move from organizing a sequence of model calls to supporting a continuous loop of acting, observing, and learning. A framework can help a model use tools and manage a workflow, but the agent still needs to recognize when an approach is failing, revise its plan, and verify whether it actually achieved the goal.

That also changes the relationship between the framework and the model. We should ask which capabilities belong in the model itself and which need explicit support from the surrounding system. Planning, memory, and error recovery probably need both. The framework should make useful feedback available, and the model should be able to learn from it.

For me, the important measure is whether an agent can complete a long task reliably, with an appropriate amount of human involvement. Building more elaborate workflows is useful only if it improves that outcome.
